title: Everything We Learned in 29 minutes at Goldman Sachs: the 10 commandments (part 1)
summary: Jean digs out a 15-year-old sheet from her first day of Goldman Sachs analyst training, 'Top 10 Tips for Success at Goldman Sachs', and the sisters dissect rules one through five: manage your own career, defy intellectual boredom, build your network broadly, hold yourself to the highest standards, and never talk business in the elevator. They mix Goldman lore (how Jean was recruited to Zynga via peer friends, 'headline risk', immaculate slides) with Cherie's tech-world counterpoints on speed and capturing wins.

ideas.idea: Manage your own career: no one cares more about your career than you do and no one will promote you on a whim, so be intentional and proactive.
ideas.detail: Rule one on the Goldman Sachs University training sheet; at a big company Cherie mapped herself against the internal PM promotion ladder criteria, while at startups without HR guidelines you must create visibility yourself.
names_or_cases: Goldman Sachs University 'Top 10 Tips for Success'

ideas.idea: Keep a 'wins' folder on your work computer with screenshots of every kudos email and strong deliverable, for promotion packets and for bad days.
ideas.detail: Cherie's manager told her to do this at LinkedIn; Jean says she never did because Goldman's grind culture left no time, and admits it is not hard, just annoying, but the better way.

ideas.idea: Grinding hard is not enough; you need proof and testimonials captured along the way to be recognized for your work.
ideas.detail: Cherie contrasts her 'zillennial' expectation of recognition with the millennial finance culture where having no life was a point of pride and good work was rewarded with more work piled on.

ideas.idea: Defy intellectual boredom by assigning yourself homework that follows your interests and adds value to your team.
ideas.detail: On Goldman's internal fund-of-funds team Jean invented a daily news write-up on companies like Starbucks that the team then used to probe fund managers' investment theses; it also revealed her pull toward consumer tech and led to her next career.

ideas.idea: Regularly check whether you are still learning as fast as you were, and if not, introduce something to make the job engaging again since you are the captain of your own ship.
ideas.detail: Cherie noticed after her first year and a half at LinkedIn that learning had slowed and treats that as a trigger to act.

ideas.idea: As a manager, retain intellectually driven people by designing a hard, novel problem that also serves the business.
ideas.detail: Jean gave a bored data scientist a complex hypothesis to chase; the analysis ended up producing a patent, and the real motive was retention.

ideas.idea: Build your network broadly, meaning both peers and senior leaders; the two common traps are only befriending your cohort or only brown-nosing executives.
ideas.detail: You need seniors to vouch for you at promotion time, but peers go on to do incredible things and vouch for you later for startups or business school; skipping peers reads as political and alienates them.

ideas.idea: Telling peers what you want next puts you top of mind when opportunities appear; that is how Jean got recruited from Goldman to Zynga.
ideas.detail: Zynga's founder Mark Pincus (ex-finance, HBS) poached second-year analysts from Goldman's TMT banking group, reasoning Goldman, Bain and McKinsey had already screened for driven people he could teach product management; Jean only heard about the info session because banking friends knew she wanted consumer tech.

ideas.idea: Building in public and stating your goals openly beats hustling in private because people can only pull you into opportunities they know you want.
ideas.detail: The hosts contrast the 'grind is private, show up with your funding round' philosophy with their own approach of sharing ups and downs and goals.

ideas.idea: In traditional finance the decision-makers are much older, making senior relationships more intimidating than in tech where seniors are close to your age.
ideas.detail: Jean made fewer close senior connections at Goldman than Cherie did at LinkedIn for this reason.

ideas.idea: Hold yourself to the highest standard the firm does: act as an emissary of the firm and apply the 'headline risk' test to everything you do, at work or outside.
ideas.detail: Goldman drilled analysts to ask whether they would be comfortable seeing their action on the front page of the New York Times or Wall Street Journal; Jean says it made analysts paranoid but kept them conscious of doing right by the company.

ideas.idea: Goldman's perfectionism, where slides were corrected to the tenth of a millimeter, instilled a lasting pride in work and operational excellence that many younger workers lack.
ideas.detail: Jean still proofreads emails far longer than Cherie; she argues everything you put out should clear a bar of greatness even if you move fast.

ideas.idea: Speed of iteration matters too: a startup-bred VP sent typo-filled emails from his iPhone and got faster responses, so balance excellence against speed.
ideas.detail: Cherie's LinkedIn VP would screenshot, circle and send feedback instantly; the hosts agree it is a balance and that different people hold different bars.

ideas.idea: Never talk business in the elevator, sauna or any small shared space, because you never know who is listening.
ideas.detail: At Goldman a leaked secret could blow up a deal worth hundreds of millions, and the elevator might hold reporters, the other side of a deal, or someone who could trade on the information; Cherie was approached after naming someone in an LA sauna.

ideas.idea: New grads with zero professional experience need explicit training on what is and isn't okay, and simple printed rules like these still hold up 15 years later.
ideas.detail: The sheet came from Goldman Sachs University's 2010 first-year analyst training packet; Jean kept it pinned on a bulletin board through every move.
